Great — I'll run a mock interview. Here's the first question:

"Walk me through your resume — highlight the experiences that make you a strong fit for a financial analyst role and a specific project where you drove impact."

Answer as you would in the room (typed). After your answer I'll score it on structure, evidence and specificity and give one concrete improvement, then I'll ask the next question.

Score: 2/10.

Why: Structure is weak (no clear S-T-A-R). Evidence is missing — no result, metric or outcome. Specificity is low: you didn't name the company/context, your role, the timeframe, or the tools you used.

Concrete rewrite (2–3 sentences, STAR-focused) you can say instead — fill the brackets with your facts:
"In my role at [Company], I was asked to produce a monthly forecast after a pricing change reduced visibility of unit sales (Situation/Task). I built a three-statement model in [your skill] that started from unit and price revenue drivers, ran three scenarios, and reconciled projections to public comps and prior quarters (Action). The model improved forecast accuracy by [X%] versus the prior process and supported a pricing recommendation the CFO adopted, which we estimated would raise annual EBITDA by [Y%] (Result)."
One concrete improvement: add a measured result (X% or a dollar amount) or, if none was tracked, state a concrete qualitative outcome you achieved (e.g., "the CFO adopted it" or "reduced forecast variance from ±15% to ±6% in the next quarter").

Next question (ready when you are): "Tell me about a time you found an error in a model or report. What happened and how did you fix it?"

You did the bare minimum: 3/10.

Why: You answered the prompt (three-statement model + comps) but gave only a high-level plan — no Situation/Task, no Actions you personally took, no tools or methods, and no Result or impact. Interviewers hear that as "I know the basics" not "I did it and drove outcomes."

What to fix next (one concrete change): add one measured outcome or decision your work changed (a percent, dollar, variance reduction, or an executive decision you influenced). If you truly lack metrics, add a tight qualitative outcome plus the timeframe (e.g., "CFO adopted it within two weeks").
Quick rewrite to use in the next interview (2–3 sentences; fill brackets once):  
"In my role at [Company], I built a three-statement model after [specific trigger] to replace an unreliable forecasting process (S/T). I modeled revenue from unit and price drivers in Excel, stress-tested scenarios, and reconciled to public comps and the prior quarter (A). The model cut forecast variance from ±[old]% to ±[new]% within the next quarter and was used to support a pricing change that increased EBITDA by ~[Y]% annually (R)."

One question: pick one metric to add — which do you have: forecast variance change, EBITDA impact, or a decision adopted?

replies:
You don't have a resume on file here yet. Paste your resume (or paste the Experience, Skills, and Education sections) and I'll read it and save every entry as draft facts.

If you want a quick checklist to compare your resume against common Junior Software Engineer requirements while you paste it, here are the high-impact items to include or improve (I'll assume you want full-stack unless you tell me front- or back-end):
1. Clear headline and contact
- One-line desired title (e.g., "Junior Software Engineer") plus email, phone, GitHub and LinkedIn (if public).
2. Short goal/summary (1 line)
- Tie your past experience to the role: what you want to build and the stack you target.
3. Experience or projects with measurable outcomes
- For each job or project: one line context (what the system did), 2–4 bullets showing what you built, the tech used (languages, frameworks, tools), and one concrete result or metric where possible (reduced load time by X, increased test coverage to Y, shipped feature used by Z users). Use strong verbs: implemented, built, automated, refactored, tested, deployed. Past roles use past tense.
4. Public code and demos
- 1–3 GitHub repos or deployed apps with short notes of your role and key files or routes. Employers look for live links and README clarity.
5. Technical skills section by category
- Languages, Frameworks, Databases, Tools, Testing, Cloud. Order by strength; keep it truthful and specific (e.g., Python (Flask), JavaScript (React, Node), PostgreSQL, Docker, GitHub Actions).
6. Testing, CI/CD and engineering practices
- Show unit/integration tests, code reviews, CI pipelines, Docker, or deployment experience—even small. Junior roles expect familiarity.
7. CS fundamentals and algorithms (if you can)
- Note coursework, contest placements, or self-study (data structures, complexity, systems) if you plan to apply to companies that screen with coding interviews.
8. Education and relevant certificates
- Degree (with major and year) or bootcamp, plus relevant certifications (e.g., Coursera/edX nanodegree) and notable coursework.
9. Formatting and length
- One page (if <5 years experience), consistent bullets, readable font, ATS-friendly section titles (Experience, Projects, Skills, Education).
10. Keywords from target postings
- Include role-relevant keywords in context (e.g., REST APIs, React Hooks, SQL, Docker, AWS) but never as a keyword dump.
Two quick gaps I usually see for junior software resumes (so check these first):
- Missing metrics or concrete impact — replace vague bullets with measurable results.
- No public code or links — add at least one GitHub repo or deployed demo showing end-to-end work.

Next step: paste your resume (or the Experience, Skills, Education sections) here and I will read it, save each entry as draft facts, then tell you in two lines what I read (latest role, top skills, education) and give 2–3 specific changes to make it stronger for Junior Software Engineer roles. Do you want the resume tailored toward front-end, back-end, or full-stack? (I'll assume full-stack if you don't answer.)
